entries.name: Iterated conditional modes
entries.definition: A deterministic conditional-mode optimization algorithm that repeatedly updates one variable to a mode of its conditional distribution given the current values of the remaining variables, seeking a coordinatewise mode of a fixed joint distribution.
entries.identity_notes: ICM is a label or state optimization procedure, not the hidden Markov random field it can optimize and not iterative conditional estimation of model parameters. It is a probability-based coordinate-ascent instance related to hill climbing; Gibbs sampling instead draws a conditional random value. The classical image implementation uses local Markov neighbors and site emissions, but the conditional-mode principle also applies when an observation affects several sites or when the posterior neighborhood is wider. Single-site ICM is the defining scope; joint block updates are a stated extension. The paper credits earlier work and does not establish a 1986 first-invention claim. limitations: Initialization and update order can change the resulting mode. A coordinatewise optimum can have lower posterior probability than another configuration. ICM does not provide posterior uncertainty or the sitewise marginal posterior mode merely by returning a joint labeling.

The monotonicity and finite-state termination statements require a fixed objective, valid exact conditionals and the stated tie policy. Arbitrary switching among tied states can cycle; continuous-valued coordinate ascent need not terminate in finitely many steps.

The source’s simultaneous image updates and its changing interaction parameter are practical variants, not a proof for fully synchronous updates or a changing posterior. Alternating estimated labels and fitted parameters, especially pseudolikelihood fitting, does not inherit exact EM monotonicity.

For independent site observations, the local emission factor is sufficient for a coordinate update. Correlated observations, blur, tomography and shared likelihood factors can enlarge the required conditional neighborhood. A product containing only the updated site’s emission would then generally be wrong.

Strong coupling and fine structures can produce initialization dependence and artifacts. The illustrative interaction strength 1.5 and a few reported sweeps are not universal defaults or convergence bounds. The author’s reply explicitly limits optimality and empirical claims.

The paper’s main image examples and discussion establish method context, not universal segmentation superiority. No author code, image benchmark or parameter fitting was reproduced. A separate finite probability witness tests update order, synchronous oscillation and tie behavior.

claims.statement: For fixed observed y and model parameters theta, start at a configuration x with a defined positive posterior. In a sequential sweep, replace x_i by an element of argmax_u p(x_i=u | x_(-i),y,theta), using already updated values at earlier sites. Equivalently maximize the joint posterior with all other coordinates held fixed. For an MRF prior and independent local emissions the score is b_i(y_i|u)*p_i(u|x_neighbors); shared observation factors require every factor affected by the coordinate. Each exact update cannot decrease the fixed joint objective. On a finite configuration space, requiring strict improvement for a changed value, or retaining the current value on a tie, yields finite termination at a coordinatewise mode. This need not be a global joint MAP solution. Joint updates on conditionally independent coding sets can be parallelized; simultaneously updating interacting sites from stale neighbors has no such monotonicity guarantee. A block extension maximizes over a selected block given its complement.

entries.name: Otsu thresholding
entries.definition: A histogram-based threshold-selection algorithm that partitions ordered gray levels by maximizing class-weighted between-class variance, equivalently minimizing within-class variance for a fixed histogram.
entries.identity_notes: The binary method chooses a global intensity threshold without labeled training data or a fitted parametric intensity density. Its ordered multilevel extension jointly selects several thresholds using the same variance decomposition. It is not a supervised classifier, a learned activation threshold, adaptive spatial thresholding or a guarantee of semantically correct image segmentation. The threshold search depends on intensity counts and order, not spatial adjacency. Thresholds with the same partition can be equivalent even when their numeric values differ. limitations: An empty histogram has no probability distribution. A constant-intensity histogram has no admissible nonempty binary split and has zero total variance, so the separability ratio is undefined without an added convention. Implementations must state how they handle these cases.

Multiple thresholds can maximize the objective. The paper does not prescribe a universal tie rule such as averaging all maximizing thresholds. Quantization, bin selection and intensity transformations can affect the result; the stated invariance is for corresponding affine intensity transformations, not arbitrary nonlinear remapping.

Section III D suggests that the objective is always unimodal while acknowledging no proof. That universal claim is not adopted: the original finite histogram with equal counts at 0, 10, 11, 21 has two separated maximizing threshold plateaus with a lower objective at 10. A full scan preserves the global objective; an assumed-unimodal local search need not.

The variance criterion measures statistical separation in intensity space. It does not require visibly bimodal histograms and does not ensure that the selected classes correspond to the desired objects. Spatial connectivity, texture and semantic labels are absent from this objective.
The multilevel criterion requires a joint ordered-threshold optimization or another justified optimizer. The linear scan complexity above is for the binary case, not every multilevel search.

The three small illustrative character, texture and cell images are application examples, not a modern accuracy benchmark or a universal comparison. The PDF shares pages with unrelated articles and a book review; those passages are excluded from evidence. No author implementation or image evaluation was run.

claims.statement: For nonnegative counts n_i at ordered gray levels i with positive total N, use p_i=n_i/N and total mean mu_T=sum_i i*p_i. For every binary threshold k admitting two nonempty classes, set w=sum_(i<=k) p_i and m=sum_(i<=k) i*p_i. Compute between-class variance B(k)=(mu_T*w-m)^2/[w*(1-w)] and choose a global maximizer. Cumulative counts and first moments give an O(L) scan over L gray levels after histogram construction. At fixed total variance T, within-class variance is T-B(k); if T>0, maximizing the separability ratio B(k)/T gives the same maximizers. The source’s multilevel extension jointly partitions the ordered levels into nonempty classes and maximizes sum_c w_c*(mu_c-mu_T)^2; recursive binary splitting is not automatically equivalent to that joint optimum.

entries.name: Wavelet-domain hidden Markov model
entries.definition: A statistical wavelet-coefficient model family using latent mixture states to represent coefficient distributions and Markov dependencies among those states to capture within-scale clustering or cross-scale persistence.
entries.identity_notes: This is the wavelet-domain framework of Crouse, Nowak and Baraniuk, including independent-mixture, within-scale hidden-chain and cross-scale hidden-tree constructions. The independent mixture is its no-dependence special case. The source also discusses richer hidden graphs; a generic family member is not necessarily a sequential HMM or a Bayesian network with the same graph. Generic hidden Markov trees and chains provide structural components, while wavelet coefficients, mixture emissions and scale organization specify this family. A trained parameter instance, a wavelet transform alone, wavelet shrinkage in general and a neural hidden layer are different identities. limitations: Wavelet decorrelation does not imply independence. Zero-mean conditional Gaussian coefficients can be uncorrelated while their squared magnitudes remain dependent through hidden states. Marginalizing the states does not generally leave an observed Markov process.

The two zero-mean states and chosen graph are modeling choices, not universal properties of wavelets. More states, nonzero means and alternative emissions are possible. Scaling coefficients may be modeled separately or left unchanged in a particular application. Directed dependence does not establish intervention causality.

With K states and dense transitions, exact chain/tree message cost is O(edges*K^2). Richer or loopy graphs need separate inference and complexity analysis; linearity in graph size for chordal models also depends on bounded clique and state sizes. Parameter tying imposes equality constraints and requires pooled sufficient statistics with proper normalization.

Exact EM under suitable model and optimization conditions does not ensure a global likelihood optimum. Empty posterior components, zero transition occupancy, singular Gaussian variances and constrained parameters need explicit handling. The record does not certify an author implementation or fit any parameters.

Appendix A in the inspected 1997 preprint contains inconsistent parent/child epsilon indices in Equations (19) and(22), a finest/coarsest initialization typo and missing or inconsistent state indices in the downward recursion. This record uses the stated normalized model factorization; an asymmetric three-node finite example verifies consistent messages against complete enumeration rather than copying those displays literally.

The denoising formula assumes the stated orthonormal transform and independent white Gaussian noise. Subtracting a noise estimate from fitted noisy variances and clipping at zero is a plug-in procedure, not a general constrained-maximum-likelihood theorem. The zero signal-variance boundary is degenerate. Estimated parameters and noise are treated as fixed, rather than integrated out.

Reported denoising, classification and change-detection examples do not establish universal superiority. Table 1 does not make the tree best for every signal, and selected comparator numbers are imported from other work. Comparing class likelihoods alone assumes the appropriate prior-and-cost threshold is one; unequal priors or costs generally change that threshold.

The fully inspected source is the 31-page author preprint revised August 1997. The 1998 journal article DOI 10.1109/78.668544 is corroborating bibliographic context, not an assertion that those journal PDF bytes were read. No first-invention date, benchmark reproduction or author-code execution is asserted.

claims.statement: Transform a signal into wavelet coefficients W_i and assign each coefficient a finite hidden mixture state S_i. Given all states, the coefficient emissions factor by site. The canonical two-state emission uses zero-mean Gaussian components with a narrow and a wide variance. A hidden chain models within-scale dependence; a hidden tree models parent-to-child persistence across scales. For a rooted tree, p(s,w)=pi(s_root)*product_edges A_child(s_child|s_parent)*product_i N(w_i;mu_i(s_i),v_i(s_i)), with normalized root and transition laws and positive emission variances. Upward subtree likelihoods and a downward pass yield exact node and edge state posteriors for a tree; chains admit the corresponding forward/backward inference. Those expectations support EM updates and optional parameter tying over explicitly selected sites or scales. In the source’s orthonormal-wavelet additive white Gaussian noise model, noise variance adds to each conditional coefficient variance. For zero-mean signal components, the posterior-mean coefficient estimate averages the state-specific gain v_signal/(v_signal+v_noise) times the noisy coefficient using state probabilities conditioned on all observed coefficients in the modeled dependency component.

Abstract proposes nonparametric unsupervised histogram threshold selection by discriminant class separability, using zeroth/first cumulative moments and a multithreshold extension. SectionII printed63/PDF2: gray levels i=1..L, empirical p_i=n_i/N, nonempty finite image. For split C0=1..k and C1=k+1..L, omega=sum_i<=k p_i and mu=sum_i<=k i*p_i. Class means mu/omega and (mu_T-mu)/(1-omega). Within variance plus between variance equals fixed total variance. Optimize between variance omega(1-omega)(mu1-mu0)^2 = [mu_T*omega-mu]^2/[omega(1-omega)] over valid nonempty classes0<omega<1. Sequential complete threshold scan; normalization eta=between/total has same optimum when total>0. Cumulative updates make threshold scanning linear in number of bins after histogram construction.

limitations: The complete-data estimator must be defined on posterior-supported completed data and have the required moments. Empty mixture components, boundary or infinite MLEs, constrained parameter spaces and nonidentifiability need explicit conventions; a conditional mean can leave a nonconvex parameter space.

Conditional expectation is the least-squares approximation to an integrable squared-error target under a fixed law. That fact does not prove decreasing true parameter error, observed-likelihood monotonicity or global convergence across ICE iterations with changing laws.

The Delmas equivalence uses the mean/expectation parameter psi, although the source calls it canonical; its natural parameter phi is distinct. For Gaussian mixtures, expectation of a complete-data class mean or variance containing a random class count differs in general from a ratio of expected sufficient statistics. The usual Gaussian-parameter ICE update therefore cannot simply be replaced by an EM update without checking the conditions.

Monte Carlo approximation requires valid posterior sampling and appropriate convergence conditions. Correlated Gibbs samples, finite sample counts and apparently steady parameters do not by themselves certify exact expectations or convergence. native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes exact conditional resampling, including fixed coordinate cycles and fixed random-scan mixtures. It is a sampling procedure, not a Gibbs distribution, Markov random field, annealing schedule or conditional maximization method. Metropolis-within-Gibbs replaces some exact conditional draws by invariant transitions and is represented separately. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 159 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Ignored-inclusive full-checkout searches found prior discovery leads for Gibbs and slice sampling plus unrelated environment substring hits, not existing concept records. Existing HMM/MRF models and general Metropolis–Hastings were inspected to distinguish model, general transition and specialized algorithm scope.
limitations: The full conditional distributions must be compatible with a proper joint target and be sampled correctly. An approximate conditional draw is not automatically an exact Gibbs step.
Target invariance alone does not establish irreducibility, aperiodicity, convergence from every start or rapid mixing. Coordinate dependence and disconnected support can obstruct exploration.

The finite positive-state convergence theorem in Geman and Geman has explicit site-visit and positivity assumptions; it is not a theorem for every continuous, constrained or parallel Gibbs implementation.
Simultaneously updating dependent coordinates using stale neighbors is outside the stated sequential mechanism; valid parallel or adaptive scan schemes need separate arguments.
Fixed-temperature posterior sampling and a cooling schedule for optimization are different procedures. No universal convergence rate or image-restoration performance is asserted.

native_neighbors.name: Simulated annealing
native_neighbors.definition: A stochastic optimization procedure that explores candidate configurations with temperature-controlled acceptance of cost-increasing moves and progressively cools that acceptance process to concentrate search on low-cost configurations.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the temperature-scheduled optimization procedure exemplified by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi. Its basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis step is distinguished from fixed-temperature target sampling, generic annealing metaphors, training signal annealing and a proof that a particular finite schedule reaches a global minimum. The 1983 article is a primary formulation, not a claim of exclusive invention. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The exp(−delta/T) expression is for positive effective temperature with the physical Boltzmann constant absorbed into its cost units. Zero temperature is a limiting or separately defined greedy rule, not evaluation of that quotient at T=0. Equal-cost moves are accepted in the displayed symmetric-proposal rule.

At fixed T the Boltzmann interpretation requires a proper target and a valid transition construction. Arbitrary asymmetric proposals do not justify dropping the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio. Lowering T changes the target; stationarity for a fixed stage does not imply equilibrium throughout a finite cooling run.

Positive-temperature uphill acceptance only permits escape through moves supported by the proposal. It does not ensure reaching every state, escaping a local basin in a chosen budget or tracking equilibrium. Rapid cooling can freeze search prematurely; schedule length, cost scale, move connectivity and constraints matter.

The primary article’s heuristics and empirical scaling claims are not a finite-run global-convergence theorem or a universal complexity bound. The later mathematical conditions for asymptotic annealing convergence were not audited here. No electronic-design or traveling-salesman benchmark is reproduced.

claims.statement: Choose a representation of feasible configurations, an objective E to minimize, a random rearrangement proposal and an annealing schedule specifying temperatures and work at each temperature. At current configuration x, propose y and compute delta=E(y)−E(x). For the basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis rule at effective temperature T>0 measured in cost units, accept delta<=0 moves and accept delta>0 with probability exp(−delta/T); otherwise retain x. Repeat transitions at the current temperature, then lower temperature according to the schedule. High temperatures permit larger cost-increasing moves more frequently; cooling reduces that probability. The source motivates sufficient equilibration at each stage. Candidate representation, move set and schedule depend on the optimization problem; the returned low-cost configuration is a search result rather than a certified global minimizer.

native_neighbors.identity_notes: This is Freitag and Al-Onaizan’s absolute threshold pruning rule. It uses an additive score difference, unlike their relative-score and last-token relative thresholds. It is an additional local pruning step, not a stopping certificate or a method that automatically widens the beam. A positive margin is required to retain the best finite-scoring item under the printed non-strict inequality; a zero margin would discard even maximum-score candidates.
The procedure is layered onto a decoder with its own EOS and width policy. It does not by itself specify the entire decoder or guarantee improved speed or quality.
